newsitem.title: PERU: Peru offers $75,000 for information on MRTA leader.
newsitem.headline: Peru offers $75,000 for information on MRTA leader.

text.p: Peru's police on Saturday offered a $75,000 reward for information leading to the capture of the man they believe could be the Tupac Amaru rebels' new leader after last month's bloody end to the group's hostage-taking.

A full-page advertisement in the pro-government daily Expreso announced the offer would even include a pardon for anyone providing information from their prison cell about Hugo Avellaneda, the group's former international spokesman.

President Alberto Fujimori tipped Avellaneda -- the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movment's (MRTA) best known member still at large -- as the rebel most likely to take control of the group after commandos killed leader Nestor Cerpa in a hostage rescue.

The reward may be worth 650 times Peru's minimum monthly wage but seems insignificant compared to the $1 million bounty the police put on the leader of the bloodier rebel group Shining Path, Abimael Guzman, until his 1992 capture.

The publication of the reward also displayed five passport photographs of Avellaneda depicting an intellectual-looking rebel wearing glasses in fuzzy-haired portraits showing him clean shaven, bearded and with a moustache.

Following Cerpa's death in a military raid at the Japanese ambassador's home on April 22 to rescue 72 hostages held by rebels, key MRTA members gathered at a meeting in the group's central jungle heartland, anti-terrorist reports said.

According to the documents obtained by Reuters, the men most likely to replace Cerpa were "Comrade Alejandro" and Avellaneda. Alejandro was believed to be the same rebel who told Reuters from a secret location in February he was the military leader in the central jungle, where the MRTA has its only permanently armed members.

Avellaneda acted for three years as MRTA spokesman for the group from Paris until 1995, when Cerpa visited him and told him of the group's decision that he "perform a new role outside Europe," current international spokesman Isaac Velazco said.
Analysts believe the MRTA counts on fewer than 200 armed members.
